subject: mathematics
question_text: Let R be the relation defined on the set of all natural numbers N by R = {(x, y) : x, y ∈ N, 2x + y = 41}. Find R and check whether it is (i) reflexive, (ii) symmetric and (iii) transitive.

mark_split.label: Find R and its 20 ordered pairs

NOTE ON THE CONVENTION: N is taken as {1, 2, 3, …}, which is the Telangana Intermediate convention, giving x = 1 to 20 and 20 pairs. If a syllabus counted 0 as a natural number the list would gain (0, 41) and hold 21 pairs, but all three verdicts below would be unchanged. The three counterexamples were each checked by substitution: 2(1) + 1 = 3, 2(39) + 1 = 79, and 2(12) + 7 = 31, none of which is 41.

recall_prompt: Say how you would answer this — say how you bound x, and what you would produce to settle each of the three properties.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Find R and its 20 ordered pairs
steps.margin_note: First mark. The bound x ≤ 20 and at least the first and the last pair must be on the page.
lines: y ∈ N needs 41 − 2x ≥ 1, that is 2x ≤ 40, so x ≤ 20. Also x ≥ 1.
So x = 1, 2, 3, …, 20 and R has 20 ordered pairs.

recall.must_convey: That y = 41 − 2x must stay in N, which forces x ≤ 20, giving the 20 pairs from (1, 39) to (20, 1).
accept: make y the subject and require y to be at least one so x is at most twenty
x runs from one to twenty so there are twenty pairs
the pairs start at one thirty nine and end at twenty one
y equals forty one minus two x, y natural kavali kabatti x twenty varaku
list R as ordered pairs not as an equation

steps.why: y has to be a natural number, and that single requirement is what stops x at 20. Without it the equation would give an endless list, and R would not be a set of pairs that can be written down.
common_mistakes: Letting x run past 20, which gives y = −1 and other values outside N.
Taking x = 0, which is not in N under the convention N = {1, 2, 3, …}.
Writing R as the equation 2x + y = 41 instead of as a set of ordered pairs.
steps.memory_tip: Make y the subject, then push x up until y would drop below 1 — that is where the list stops.

steps.label: Test the three properties
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Each verdict needs its own counterexample written out; a bare "not reflexive" earns nothing.
lines: (i) Reflexive: (x, x) ∈ R would need 2x + x = 41, so x = 41/3, which is not in N.
For example 2(1) + 1 = 3 ≠ 41, so (1, 1) ∉ R. Hence R is not reflexive.
so (12, 7) ∉ R. Hence R is not transitive.

lines.text: ∴ R is neither reflexive, nor symmetric, nor transitive.

recall.must_convey: That one counterexample rejects each property: (1, 1) for reflexive, (39, 1) for symmetric, and the chain (12, 17), (17, 7) with (12, 7) missing for transitive.
accept: no pair of the form x x works because three x equals forty one has no natural solution
one thirty nine is in R but thirty nine one is not so it is not symmetric
twelve seventeen and seventeen seven are in R but twelve seven is not
prathi property ki oka counterexample chupinchali
none of the three properties holds

steps.why: One counterexample settles each property, and each counterexample must use pairs that really are in R. For transitivity that means finding a chain (x, y) and (y, z) both inside R first, which is why 17 is used twice.
common_mistakes: Calling R symmetric because 2x + y = 41 looks balanced; the coefficients 2 and 1 are different, so swapping x and y changes the sum.
Testing reflexivity with a pair such as (1, 39) instead of a pair of the form (x, x).
Calling R transitive without first finding a chain (x, y) and (y, z) that both lie in R.
steps.memory_tip: To reject a property you need one pair; to accept it you must argue for every pair.
